activities.prompt: Without looking, explain this objective in course terms: Identify the anatomical locations and major functions of neural structures in the brainstem respiratory centers.
activities.expectedAnswer: The medullary dorsal respiratory group is predominantly inspiratory and receives sensory input through the nucleus tractus solitarius; the ventral group is recruited especially for forced expiration and contains rhythm-generating complexes. Pontine pneumotaxic and apneustic centers modify inspiration, while cortex and limbic/hypothalamic inputs can override the basic pattern.

activities.prompt: Without looking, explain this objective in course terms: Identify the locations of central and peripheral chemoreceptors and predict their responses to changes in arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH.
activities.expectedAnswer: Central chemoreceptors in the brainstem respond mainly to CO2-driven CSF H+ and dominate most ventilatory conditions. Peripheral carotid and aortic bodies use glomus cells to detect low PaO2, high PaCO2, and low pH; hypoxemia closes O2-sensitive K+ channels, depolarizes the cell, opens Ca2+ channels, and increases afferent signaling.

activities.prompt: Without looking, explain this objective in course terms: Describe the three major sensory-receptor types in the lungs and airways, their vagal afferents, primary stimuli, and physiologic functions.
activities.expectedAnswer: Slowly adapting stretch receptors signal inflation and can terminate inspiration. Rapidly adapting irritant receptors provoke cough and bronchoconstriction. Juxtacapillary receptors/bronchial C fibers respond to interstitial congestion or noxious stimuli with rapid shallow breathing, bronchoconstriction, and sometimes mucus secretion; lung afferents travel mainly in the vagus.

activities.prompt: Without looking, explain this objective in course terms: Describe how arterial oxygen and carbon dioxide alter alveolar ventilation and the synergistic effects when both change simultaneously.
activities.expectedAnswer: Ventilation rises approximately linearly with CO2 over the operating range and rises steeply when oxygen falls below about 60 mmHg. Hypoxemia steepens the CO2 response, and hypercapnia increases the ventilatory response to low oxygen, so simultaneous abnormalities produce a synergistic drive.

items: Afferent signaling to the medulla increases
activities.rationale: This is the glomus-cell stimulus-response chain shown in the lecture.

activities.prompt: Order the central-chemoreceptor pathway that links an arterial CO2 rise to increased ventilation.
items: Carbonic anhydrase in CSF generates H+
Central chemoreceptors sense the pH/H+ change
activities.rationale: The lecturer emphasized that charged H+ and bicarbonate do not readily cross the blood-brain barrier; soluble CO2 crosses, is converted in CSF, and drives central chemoreceptors through H+.

activities.prompt: A patient develops pulmonary edema and begins breathing rapidly and shallowly with bronchoconstriction. Which receptor response best matches the lecture?
activities.rationale: Pulmonary edema was the lecture prototype for J-receptor/C-fiber activation, producing rapid shallow breathing and bronchoconstriction; bronchial C fibers can also promote mucus secretion.

activities.prompt: Which blood-gas combination should produce the greatest ventilatory drive in the course framework?
activities.rationale: PaCO2 normally drives ventilation, PaO2 produces a steep response below about 60 mmHg, and simultaneous hypoxemia plus hypercapnia produces synergistic drive.
